They say he was born from a wave that forgot to break, and that he stood on nothing at all, for in those days there was no land, only the grey sea chewing on itself. Hungry, he cast a line woven from his own hair, baited with a song his mother had never sung. Something vast took the hook. For seven nights he hauled, and on the eighth the sea gave up its jaw: a great drowned skull rising white and gleaming, its teeth jutting above the water in a crooked row.

The fisherman wept, for he had wanted only a meal, and his tears were the first salt. Where they fell on the teeth, moss grew, then palms, then birds who laughed at him. He built his hut upon the largest molar. Still the islands shift, the elders say, because the jaw is not dead, only patient, and one day it will close.
